title: The Sharpe Pint

opening_mood.text: Morning all. Grab your flat white and find a quiet corner, because the macro picture has decided to get very noisy, very quickly. From military exchanges in the Gulf to central bankers in hospital and a massive shift in how the AI boom is being funded, there is plenty to get through before the market open.

Today, we are looking at why the AI trade is moving from equity hype to hard-nosed infrastructure debt, how to avoid a classic EV/EBITDA interview trap, and a clever statistical trick to find hidden relationships between stocks. Let's get stuck in.

content.text: The geopolitical risk premium is back with a vengeance, and the macro desk is going to have a busy morning. Here is what you need to know before the trading day kicks off.
1. US-Iran Strikes & Strait of Hormuz Closure: Markets Brace for Energy Shock

The US military has launched self-defence strikes against Iran following the downing of an Apache attack helicopter near the Strait of Hormuz, which President Donald Trump blamed on Tehran. The critical waterway, which handles about 25% of the world's seaborne oil, has been effectively closed since late February. Brent crude is hovering around $91.78 a barrel, up from $70 before the conflict began. The escalation triggered a tech-led sell-off on Wall Street, with the Nasdaq falling nearly 1% and the S&P 500's tech sector dropping 2%, which spilled over to Asia and Europe. The FTSE 100 fell 1.4% on Tuesday to close at 10,227.33, though it edged up slightly on Wednesday morning.

Why it matters: While the FTSE 100 has a natural hedge through its heavy weighting in energy majors like BP and Shell, the broader market is sweating over the supply-chain impact of a closed Strait of Hormuz. The upcoming US CPI report on June 10 is the next big catalyst, with fears that energy costs will drive inflation higher. If energy costs start bleeding into core inflation, the Fed's rate-cut cycle is officially dead in the water.
2. Morgan Stanley Forecasts AI Debt Supercycle to Top $500bn in 2026

Morgan Stanley projects that global AI-related debt issuance will more than double to nearly $570 billion in 2026. Hyperscalers like Alphabet, Amazon, Microsoft, and Meta are turning to bond markets to fund their massive AI capex, which is expected to hit $700 billion this year and surpass $1 trillion in 2027. AI-related debt is approaching 15% of the US investment-grade corporate market.

Why it matters: AI is no longer just an equity story; it is reshaping global credit markets. Hyperscalers that have long relied on strong cash flows are increasingly turning to debt financing as investment needs surge. Credit investors are moving from vague enthusiasm for chatbots to demanding collateral, contracts, and predictable usage, such as GPU-backed loans and data centre leasing cash flows. For fixed-income and private credit desks, the game now is underwriting physical assets like GPUs and data centres rather than just betting on software multiples.
3. Bank of Japan Governor Kazuo Ueda Hospitalised Ahead of Critical June Meeting

BOJ Governor Kazuo Ueda has been hospitalised with an infected liver cyst and will miss the June 15-16 monetary policy meeting. He is expected to be in the hospital for about two weeks. Deputy Governor Ryozo Himino will chair the meeting, and Deputy Governor Shinichi Uchida will host the press conference.

Why it matters: The BOJ was widely expected to raise its short-term policy rate to 1% from 0.75% at next week's meeting, taking borrowing costs to levels unseen in three decades. Ueda's absence injects fresh uncertainty into the yen and Japanese government bonds (JGBs). While the deputy governors are capable, executing Japan's most significant rate hike in three decades without the Governor on the bridge is a tough sell. Expect the yen to face some short-term volatility as traders bet on a delay.
4. Eli Lilly's $25B+ M&A Spree Dominates Pharma Consolidation
Eli Lilly has spent $25.27 billion across 10 transactions in 2026 so far, capturing over half of the $46.38 billion spent by the top 12 global pharmaceutical companies by revenue this year.

Why it matters: Lilly is using the massive cash flows generated by its blockbuster obesity drugs, Mounjaro and Zepbound, to aggressively buy out biotech firms, securing its long-term pipeline. It is a classic winner-takes-all dynamic where the obesity giants are outbidding traditional pharma peers for early-stage biotech assets, effectively running a biotech venture fund on an unprecedented scale.
5. WH Smith Shares Plunge 17% on Profit Warning and 20% Capital Raise

WH Smith shares crashed 17% on the FTSE 250 after the travel retailer cut its full-year headline pre-tax profit guidance to 75 million to 90 million pounds, down from April's guidance of 90 million to 105 million pounds, and announced plans to raise capital by issuing up to 26 million new shares, representing 20% of its share capital.

Why it matters: The company blamed a decline in passenger numbers and weakening consumer demand across its travel divisions, with Middle East flight disruptions due to the ongoing Iran conflict hitting its airport stores. WH Smith has been a darling of the travel retail pivot story, but this profit warning shows how vulnerable travel-reliant businesses are to geopolitical shocks and consumer belt-tightening.
6. UK Government Releases Billions in Pension Surpluses to Boost Economy
UK Pensions Minister Torsten Bell launched a consultation on June 10, 2026, to allow trustees to safely release Defined Benefit pension scheme surpluses to employers and members.

Why it matters: Defined Benefit schemes are in their strongest financial position in a generation, with surpluses quadrupling over the last five years due to higher interest rates. The new proposals aim to give trustees flexibility to release these funds, potentially freeing up billions of pounds for corporate investment and the wider UK economy. For years, pensions were a black hole of deficits that killed M&A deals. Now, the prospect of releasing surpluses could make companies with large Defined Benefit schemes highly attractive targets.

sections.title: Markets Briefing: What Moved and Why

content.text: The Intraday Whiplash

If you spent Tuesday afternoon staring at your screens wondering if your Bloomberg terminal had developed a serious case of the jitters, you weren't alone. Wall Street went on a proper rollercoaster, with the S&P 500 swinging from a 1% gain in early trading to a stomach-churning 2.3% drop by midday, before some late-afternoon bargain hunting dragged it back to close down a modest 0.3% at 7,386.65. The tech-heavy Nasdaq took the brunt of the pain, sliding 1% to 25,678.82, while the Dow managed to eke out a 0.2% gain to 50,872.11. Meanwhile, the Russell 2000 rose 0.4% to 2,867.02, showing that beneath the surface of the tech carnage, the rest of the market was actually trying to hold its ground.
The Crowded Trade Shakeout

What’s driving this schizophrenia? It’s the classic rhythm of a heavily crowded trade getting violently shaken out. The semiconductor and AI darlings—Nvidia, AMD, and Apple—are whipsawing like a small dinghy in a North Sea gale. One day they’re up 5%, the next they’re down 9%. Investors are starting to ask the uncomfortable question: when do these astronomical capital expenditures actually turn into cold, hard GAAP profits? It's no longer enough to just whisper 'AI' and watch the market cap swell by a hundred billion. Traders are demanding receipts, and until they get them, expect the volatility to remain dialled up to eleven.
Geopolitics and the Oil Spurt

Adding fuel to the fire is a genuine flare-up in geopolitical risk. The US and Iran have traded direct military strikes after an American helicopter was downed near the Strait of Hormuz, throwing a spanner in the works of any hopes for a quick ceasefire. Brent crude is back up to $91.78 a barrel, and WTI is sitting at $88.31. If you're looking for a cross-asset read, look at gold—interestingly, it has slipped below its 200-day moving average for the first time since 2023, suggesting that even traditional safe havens are getting messy as liquidity gets squeezed and investors scramble for cash.
The SpaceX Elephant in the Room

But let’s be honest: the real reason everyone on the trading floor is distracted is the absolute monster of an elephant in the room. SpaceX is going public this Friday (12 June) under the ticker SPCX. This isn't just an IPO; it’s a systemic event. Elon Musk is looking to raise $75 billion at a fixed price of $135 per share, implying a valuation of roughly $1.75 trillion to $1.77 trillion. To put that in perspective, it’s more than double the record set by Saudi Aramco in 2019. The order book is reportedly oversubscribed by double, with $150 billion chasing a tiny 4% public float.

But if you dig into the S-1, the numbers are eye-watering. SpaceX posted a GAAP net loss of $4.28 billion in Q1 2026 alone. Why? Because it’s no longer just a rocket company; it’s a vertically integrated AI and connectivity behemoth. Following the merger with xAI, SpaceX is pouring billions into AI infrastructure. Interestingly, the filing revealed that Anthropic is paying SpaceX a staggering $1.25 billion a month to access compute capacity on its Colossus supercomputers. It’s a wild, high-stakes game of capital recycling, and it’s sucking a massive amount of liquidity out of the broader market just as we head into next week's crucial CPI print and FOMC meeting.
The Pub Discussion Points

items: Is the AI trade dead, or is this just a healthy flush-out? The 'down 9%, up 5%' whipsaw suggests a lot of leverage is being shaken out of the system before the next leg.

The SpaceX S-1 circularity: Anthropic paying $1.25bn/month to SpaceX for compute. Is this a genuine commercial relationship or a massive, venture-backed game of pass-the-parcel to justify a $1.75T valuation?
With Brent crude at $91.78 and geopolitical tensions rising, how long can the Fed maintain its neutral-to-dovish stance before inflation fears creep back into the bond market?

sections.title: Financial Idea of the Day: The EV/EBITDA Apples-to-Apples Trap

content.text: Why We Adjust for Minority Interests and Associates

If you have ever prepped for a corporate finance interview, you have almost certainly memorised the standard Enterprise Value (EV) formula: Equity Value plus Debt, minus Cash, plus Minority Interest. If you are lucky, you might have also remembered to subtract Associates (or Equity Method Investments). But if you ask the average junior analyst why we do this, they will usually mumble something about 'having to buy out the minority shareholders in an acquisition.' While that sounds logical, it is actually wrong—or at least, it misses the entire mathematical point.

The real reason comes down to the golden rule of valuation multiples: the numerator (EV) and the denominator (EBITDA, EBIT, or Revenue) must represent the exact same pool of assets and cash flows. If they do not, your multiple is a financial mismatch.
The Consolidation Conundrum

To understand why we adjust EV, we have to look at accounting rules. When Company A owns more than 50% of Subsidiary B, it 'controls' it. Under both IFRS and US GAAP, Company A must fully consolidate Subsidiary B's financial statements. This means Company A's income statement includes 100% of Subsidiary B's Revenue and 100% of its EBITDA, even if Company A only owns 51% of it.

Now look at the valuation multiple, EV / EBITDA. Because of consolidation, the denominator (EBITDA) includes 100% of the subsidiary's operating cash flows. But what about the numerator? The starting point for EV is Equity Value (market cap). Because the stock market is smart, Company A's share price only reflects its 51% stake in the subsidiary. The other 49% belongs to outside investors—the 'Non-controlling Interest' (NCI) or 'Minority Interest'.

If we do not adjust the numerator, we are dividing a '100% subsidiary EBITDA' denominator by a '51% subsidiary equity' numerator. To make it an apples-to-apples comparison, we must add the value of that 49% minority stake to our Enterprise Value. By doing so, both the numerator and the denominator represent 100% of the underlying operating assets.
The Reverse Problem: Associates

The exact opposite happens when Company A owns less than 50% of a business (an Associate or Equity Investment) and does not control it. In this case, Company A does not consolidate. None of the associate's Revenue or EBITDA appears in Company A's operating figures. Instead, Company A just records its share of the associate's net income way down the income statement, below the operating line.

However, the stock market still knows that Company A owns this valuable stake, so Company A's Equity Value (market cap) is higher because of it. If we calculate EV/EBITDA without adjusting, our numerator includes the value of the associate, but our denominator has 0% of the associate's EBITDA. To fix this, we must subtract the value of the Associate stake from Enterprise Value.
A Simple Numerical Example

items: Imagine Parent Co has a standalone Equity Value of £390m, £50m of Cash, and £200m of Debt. It also owns 70% of Sub Co, which is worth £100m in total.
Parent Co's standalone EBITDA is £63m, and Sub Co's EBITDA is £15m. Because Parent Co owns 70%, it consolidates Sub Co. The consolidated EBITDA on the screen is £78m (£63m + £15m).
If we calculate EV the lazy way: EV = £390m (Equity) - £50m (Cash) + £200m (Debt) = £540m. This gives us an EV/EBITDA of 6.9x (£540m / £78m).
But wait! The £390m Equity Value only reflects Parent Co's 70% share of Sub Co (worth £70m). The other 30% of Sub Co (worth £30m) belongs to minority shareholders and is not in our Equity Value.
To make it apples-to-apples, we must add the £30m Non-controlling Interest to our EV. Correct EV = £390m - £50m + £200m + £30m = £570m.
The correct EV/EBITDA is actually 7.3x (£570m / £78m). By ignoring the minority interest, we made the company look cheaper than it actually is.

content.text: Why This Matters in Asset Management and Markets

In the real world, quantitative screens and automated valuation models are notoriously bad at this. They often pull the 'book value' of minority interests or associates straight from the balance sheet because the market value of these non-listed stakes is hard to find. If a company owns a massive, highly valuable unlisted joint venture, its book value on the balance sheet might be a fraction of its true worth. This means the EV/EBITDA you see on Bloomberg or Capital IQ could be wildly distorted.

For active managers and long-short equity analysts, these accounting mismatches are where the alpha hides. If you can manually reconstruct the true Enterprise Value of a conglomerate by marking its associates and minority interests to market, you will often find mispriced assets that the passive screens miss entirely.
How to Ace This in an Interview
If an interviewer asks: 'Why do we add minority interest to Enterprise Value?' do not just say 'because we have to buy them out.' That is the amateur answer. Instead, say this:

We add minority interest to Enterprise Value to ensure numerator-denominator consistency in our valuation multiples. Because the parent company consolidates 100% of the subsidiary's operating metrics (like EBITDA) in the denominator, but the parent's equity value only reflects its partial ownership stake, we must add the value of the non-controlling interest to the numerator. This ensures both the numerator and denominator represent 100% of the subsidiary's assets.

sections.title: Quant / AI Finance Idea of the Day: Statistical Co-occurrence Contrastive Learning

content.text: If you’ve ever tried to apply deep learning to financial time series, you’ve probably hit a wall. Supervised learning is a nightmare because financial labels (like 'will this stock beat the index tomorrow?') are incredibly noisy. So, we turn to self-supervised representation learning—specifically, contrastive learning. The goal is to train a neural network to map assets into a low-dimensional embedding space where 'similar' assets are close together and 'dissimilar' ones are far apart. But how on earth do you define 'similar' for financial assets without just lazy-copying GICS sectors or getting fooled by noisy daily correlations?
The Idea: Statistical Co-occurrence Contrastive Learning

In computer vision, contrastive learning is easy: you take an image of a dog, crop it or flip it, and say 'these two are a positive pair' (similar), while an image of a bicycle is a 'negative' (dissimilar). In finance, you can't just crop a stock chart. If you define similarity using daily Pearson correlation, your model will get completely derailed by short-term market noise. If you use GICS sectors, you're not learning anything new—you're just training a very expensive neural network to mimic a spreadsheet classification from the 1990s. GICS is a bit like sorting football teams by the colour of their shirts; it misses the actual dynamics of how they play.

A brilliant paper by Rian Dolphin, Barry Smyth, and Ruihai Dong (presented at the ACM International Conference on AI in Finance) solves this with a clever statistical trick. Instead of looking at raw daily returns, they look at rolling sliding windows. For each window, they identify the top-k most similar assets to an anchor asset. Over hundreds of windows, they build a 'co-occurrence matrix'. To separate true signal from noise, they run a hypothesis test of proportions. If two assets co-occur in the top-k significantly more often than random chance, they are flagged as a robust 'positive' pair. If they co-occur significantly less, they are a 'negative' pair. This statistical filter ensures the contrastive model only learns from genuine, persistent market relationships.
Why It Matters for Asset Management

Traditional correlation matrices are notoriously unstable—as the old trading floor saying goes, 'the only thing that goes up in a crash is correlation.' By learning low-dimensional embeddings that capture long-term, statistically robust co-occurrences, you can uncover latent structures that GICS completely misses. For instance, the model might place a semiconductor manufacturer, an advanced packaging firm, and an electricity provider close together in embedding space because of their shared exposure to the AI data centre boom, even though they sit in completely different GICS sectors. When used for portfolio optimisation, these embeddings have been shown to construct portfolios with significantly lower realised volatility than those built using standard Pearson correlation.
A Quick Look at the Code

Here is a simplified Python-style illustration of how you would construct the co-occurrence matrix and use a proportion test to identify statistically robust positive and negative pairs for your contrastive loss.

import numpy as np
from scipy.stats import binomtest

# Let's say we have N assets and W rolling windows
N = 100
W = 500
k = 10  # Top-k similar assets per window

# Initialize co-occurrence matrix
C = np.zeros((N, N))

# Simulate finding top-k similar assets in each window
for w in range(W):
    for i in range(N):
        top_k_indices = np.random.choice(N, k, replace=False)
        C[i, top_k_indices] += 1

# Expected probability of co-occurrence under the null hypothesis
p_0 = k / N

# Identify robust positive and negative pairs for asset i
positives = []
negatives = []
alpha = 0.05  # Significance level
i = 0  # Let's look at the first asset

for j in range(N):
    if j == i:
        continue
    successes = C[i, j]
    
    # Test if co-occurrence is significantly higher than random chance (Positive)
    p_val_pos = binomtest(int(successes), n=W, p=p_0, alternative='greater').pvalue
    if p_val_pos < alpha:
        positives.append(j)
        
    # Test if co-occurrence is significantly lower than random chance (Negative)
    p_val_neg = binomtest(int(successes), n=W, p=p_0, alternative='less').pvalue
    if p_val_neg < alpha:
        negatives.append(j)
The Interview / Pub Conversation Angle

items: Explain that standard contrastive learning (like SimCLR) fails in finance because data augmentation (like adding noise or cropping) destroys the temporal dependencies of time series.

Introduce the concept of rolling-window co-occurrence. Explain that instead of daily correlation, you look at which assets consistently rank in each other's top-k most similar neighbours across multiple market regimes.
Explain that you use a hypothesis test of proportions (a binomial test) against a random-chance null hypothesis to mathematically define your positive and negative pairs.

Conclude with the punchline: this allows the neural network to learn a low-dimensional embedding space that captures latent, regime-hardened relationships, leading to more stable portfolio risk models and better out-of-sample diversification.

content.text: The Health Warning (Caveats)

Before you go and rewrite your entire risk model, keep a few things in mind. First, this method is computationally expensive—calculating rolling-window similarities across a universe of thousands of global equities will make your AWS bill sweat. Second, it is highly sensitive to your choice of window size and the parameter k. Finally, it struggles with sudden, structural regime shifts. If a company undergoes a massive merger or completely pivots its business model, the historical co-occurrence matrix will lag in updating, meaning your model will be trading on yesterday's relationships.

sections.title: One Article or Paper Worth Reading

content.text: The Big Five's Multi-Trillion Dollar Game of Chicken

If you have spent any time looking at tech earnings lately, you will know the capital expenditure figures are starting to look like the GDP numbers of medium-sized European nations. But are these hyperscalers being visionary, or are they driving themselves off a cliff? A fascinating NBER working paper by Jessica Wachter (Wharton) and Jonathan Wachter (Point72) titled 'What Investment Data Implies about the AI Transition' attempts to answer exactly that by reverse-engineering the math.
The Core Premise

The authors point out that the five largest US tech firms—Amazon, Alphabet, Microsoft, Meta, and Oracle—spent a staggering $380 billion on capex in 2025. They are forecast to spend roughly $755 billion in 2026, and the authors estimate this will balloon to $1.1 trillion in 2027. To put that in perspective, that is more than triple their 2024 levels. Using a two-sector open-economy model with 'rare productivity booms,' the paper asks: what kind of productivity jump do you actually need to justify this level of spending on a Net Present Value (NPV) basis?

The five largest U.S. technology firms spent $380 billion on capital expenditure in 2025 and are forecast to spend roughly double that in 2026. These firms risk bankruptcy unless expected profits grow commensurately.
The Key Takeaways

items: The 2.7x Multiplier: To justify the current capex trajectory, AI-sector productivity needs to rise by a factor of roughly 2.7x. This is an exceptionally fast productivity boom by historical standards.

The Insolvency Risk: If this productivity boom fails to materialize, these tech giants face genuine financial distress or bankruptcy. They are essentially betting their balance sheets on a massive technological breakthrough.
Macro Scenarios: If the boom does happen, it could add between 5 and 58 percentage points to cumulative US GDP growth by 2030, with AI's share of the economy reaching up to 39%.

Asset Pricing Shifts: Under their baseline calibration, the sheer scale of the AI transition pushes the risk-free rate up by 50 basis points and increases the equity risk premium by a massive 300 basis points due to the heightened systemic risk.

content.text: What to Skim vs. What to Read

Unless you are a glutton for punishment or preparing for a PhD defense, you can safely skim the heavy general equilibrium math, the calibration proofs, and the JEL-code-heavy derivations of the two-sector open-economy equations. Instead, focus your attention on the introduction, the scenario analysis tables (which outline the GDP growth paths), and the asset pricing conclusions in Section 5.
How to Use This at Work

This paper is a goldmine for anyone working in asset management, equity research, or macro strategy. It moves the AI debate away from vague hand-waving and grounds it in hard corporate finance. Next time someone at work talks about tech valuations being 'justified by future growth,' you can point out that the market is currently pricing in a coin-flip probability of a historically unprecedented 2.7x productivity miracle. If that coin lands on the wrong side, we are not just looking at a tech correction—we are looking at systemic corporate credit distress.

sections.title: People / Business Psychology Idea: Egocentric Discounting

content.text: The "I know my own homework" bias

Ever wondered why you can present a beautifully formatted, data-backed, logically flawless slide deck to your Managing Director, only for them to nod, say "good stuff", and then proceed to do exactly what they were going to do anyway? Or why, when you suggest a stock's valuation should be £100, they tweak their own estimate from £150 to £145 and call it a day?

You're witnessing Egocentric Discounting. Coined by researchers Ilan Yaniv and Eyal Kleinberger in 2000, this is the psychological tendency to heavily overweight our own initial estimates and discount the opinions of others. In classic "Judge-Advisor" experiments, researchers found that when people are given advice, they typically only adjust their initial guess by about 20% to 30% towards the advisor's recommendation—even when the advisor is a proven expert and the participant is basically guessing.

Why do we do this? It's not just pure arrogance (though in the City, that's always a solid baseline). It's a problem of asymmetric information access. You have "privileged access" to your own internal reasoning. You know exactly how you got to your number, the assumptions you made, and the logic you used. But when someone else gives you their number, you only see their conclusion, not their cognitive plumbing. Because their reasoning is a black box to you, your brain default-assumes your own shaky logic is superior to their potentially brilliant logic.
How this plays out in the City

items: The Investment Committee: A Portfolio Manager has a gut feeling that a tech stock is a buy. An analyst presents a 40-page bear case. The PM, unable to feel the analyst's internal conviction, discounts the advice, makes a token 5% reduction in position size, and keeps the trade.

The M&A Valuation: Two corporate finance teams are negotiating a deal. Team A values the target at £500m; Team B values it at £350m. Instead of finding a rational midpoint, both sides dig in, convinced the other side's model is built on "unrealistic assumptions" while their own is a work of art.

content.text: How you can use this to your advantage

items: Don't just pitch the destination; show the journey: If you want to influence a senior stakeholder, do not just hand them a conclusion. Because of egocentric discounting, they will barely budge. You must explicitly walk them through your "working out" or, better yet, co-create the assumptions with them. If they help build the logic, they won't discount it.

The 50/50 Rule for your own decisions: If you are the one making the call, recognise your own bias. If you consult an expert, don't "tweak" your model to compromise. Force yourself to mathematically average your estimate with theirs (a 50/50 split). Statistically, this simple averaging rule dramatically improves decision accuracy compared to "gut-feel" adjustments.

content.text: We discount other people's advice because we can't see their working. If you want someone to buy your conclusion, you have to let them see the plumbing.
